DECISION

DECISION 
I. 
INTRODUCTION 
A. 
SUMMARY 
The Public Utilities Regulatory Authority (Authority or PURA) approves an annual 
revenue requirement, for ratemaking purposes, for the Connecticut Natural Gas 
Corporation (CNG or Company) in the amount of $417,502,324 for the rate year, 
December 1, 2024 – November 30, 2025 (Rate Year).1  Notably, however, reflected in this 
amount is the fact that the Company will be required to return to ratepayers approximately 
$24 million of ratepayer money over the next three years; thus, the approved revenue 
requirement after such credits are extinguished is $423,824,405.  The Company may 
recover an additional $103,733 in executive compensation, provided the Company 
achieves certain performance targets.  The revenue requirement includes an allowed 
return on equity of 9.15%. 
The Company currently has authorized revenues of $442,112,779, and proposed 
a 4.46% increase, or $19,702,986, for a total revenue requirement of $461,815,765.  The 
Company’s proposal includes a 10.20% return on equity, which is above the currently 
allowed 9.30% return on equity. 
Importantly, the Company has not had a fully adjudicated rate case since 2014.  Its 
2018 rate amendment application was resolved through a settlement agreement.  Under 
the terms of that settlement agreement, the Company has continued to earn healthy 
returns, including several periods of sustained over-earning.  As a result, in 2023, the 
Authority directed the Company to file a rate amendment application or be subject to a 
financial audit.  That order precipitated this proceeding.  Further, as noted above, the 
Company is in possession of $24 million of ratepayer money. 
In this context, a reduction to the Company’s revenue requirement is not 
unexpected and was, in fact, advocated for by the Office of the Attorney General and the 
Office of Consumer Counsel.  Importantly, the Authority is bound by certain legal 
standards and is limited to the factual record before it.  For each expense, the Authority 
must find a preponderance of evidence that the expense will be incurred and that it is 
reasonable.  Here, although the Company claims it is entitled to a higher revenue 
requirement, the Company’s management did not offer sufficient evidence to support 
such a higher number. 
In an apparent effort to distract from these shortcomings, the Company has and 
will likely continue to assert unprecedented claims of bias and impropriety against the 
Authority staff.  However, the approved rate reduction is largely a mathematical function 
of the record in this proceeding, and, to the extent that record is deficient in demonstrating

B. 
BACKGROUND OF THE PROCEEDING 
CNG is a public service company within the meaning of General Statutes § 16-1.  
CNG is a subsidiary of UIL Holdings Corporation (UIL) and Avangrid Networks Inc. 
(Avangrid Networks).  Langland and Canavan Prefiled Test., Nov. 3, 2023 (Case Overview 
and Regulatory Policy Panel PFT), p. 4.2  The Company currently provides gas service 
to over 186,000 residential, commercial, and industrial customers in 25 towns and cities 
in the southwestern part of Connecticut.  Id. 
CNG previously increased its base distribution rates in 2019.  Decision, Dec. 19, 
2018, Docket No. 18-05-16, Application of Connecticut Natural Gas Corporation to 
Increase Its Rates and Charges (2018 CNG Rate Case Decision). 
On September 29, 2023, CNG submitted formal notice of its intent to file an 
application to amend its existing rate schedules. 
C. 
CONDUCT OF THE PROCEEDING 
On November 3, 2023, CNG filed an application to amend its existing rate 
schedules (Application) pursuant to General Statutes §§ 16-19 and 16-19e, Conn. 
Agencies Regs. §§ 16-1-46 and 16-1-53 et seq., and the Standard Filing Requirements 
(SFRs).  CNG’s affiliate, The Southern Connecticut Gas Company (SCG), also filed an 
application on November 3, 2023, to amend its rates. 
The Authority held a noticed scheduling conference on November 16, 2023, via 
teleconference. 
The Authority conducted a noticed revenue audit on December 11, 2023, via 
remote access, and a noticed audit of the books and records of the Company on 
December 12, 13, and 14, 2023, at the Company’s offices, 180 Marsh Hill Road, Orange, 
Connecticut. 
The Authority held two noticed in-person public comment hearings; the first on 
January 10, 2024, at the Farmington Library in Farmington, Connecticut, and the second 
on January 17, 2024, at the West Haven Public Library in West Haven, Connecticut.  The 
Authority also held one noticed virtual public comment hearing, on February 16, 2024. 
The Authority held noticed evidentiary hearings on April 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 29, and 
30, and May 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, and 8, 2023, at PURA’s offices, Ten Franklin Square, New 
Britain, Connecticut (PURA’s Offices). 
The Authority held late filed exhibit hearings on May 22 and 23, 2024, at PURA’s 
Offices.

D. 
PARTIES AND INTERVENORS 
The Authority recognized the following as parties to this proceeding: CNG, 180 
Marsh Hill Road, Orange, CT 06477; SCG, 180 Marsh Hill Road, Orange, CT 06477; the 
Office of Consumer Counsel (OCC), Ten Franklin Square, New Britain, CT 06051; the 
Authority’s Office of Education, Outreach, and Enforcement (EOE),4 Ten Franklin Square, 
New Britain, CT 06051; and the Commissioner of the Department of Energy and 
Environmental Protection (DEEP), 79 Elm Street, Hartford, CT 06106. 
The Authority designated the following as intervenors to this proceeding: the 
Connecticut Office of the Attorney General (OAG); the Connecticut Industrial Energy 
Consumers (CIEC); the United Steelworkers Local 12000; the Connecticut Independent 
Utility Workers Local 12924 (Utility Union); The Center for Children’s Advocacy (CCA); 
the Conservation Law Foundation (CLF); the Utilities Workers Union of America AFL-CIO 
Local 380; the Utility Workers Union of America A.F.L. – C.I.O. Local 470-1; and the Sierra 
Club. 
E. 
POSITION OF THE PARTIES 
The Company seeks a revenue requirement increase of $19,702,986 representing 
a 4.46% increase in distribution revenue.  Application, p. 2; Late Filed Ex. 1, Att. 2, Sch. 
A-1.0.  In addition, CNG proposed a 10.20% return on equity (ROE).  CNG Brief, p. 3. 
EOE actively participated in this proceeding, issuing over 400 interrogatories, 
providing expert testimony, conducting cross examination during the evidentiary and late 
filed exhibit hearings, and filing a brief.  EOE recommends that the Authority reject several 
portions of CNG’s requested revenue requirement increase.  EOE Brief, p. 1.  EOE also 
dedicates a significant portion of its brief to arguing that there are myriad problems with 
CNG’s customer service performance, which it argues warrants a reduction to the 
Company’s allowed ROE.  Id., p. 38.  In addition, EOE recommends that the Authority 
allow the Company an ROE of 8.28%, which represents the midpoint of a range of 8.08% 
and 8.49%, as recommended by Aaron Rothschild, EOE’s witness.  Id., pp. 1, 21. 
OCC also actively participated in this proceeding, issuing hundreds of 
interrogatories, providing expert testimony, conducting cross examination during the

F. 
PUBLIC COMMENT 
The Authority held two public comment hearings, one in-person and one virtual.  
CNG presented a PowerPoint explaining its request at the start of each session before 
the admission of any public comment. 
The in-person public comment hearing specific to the CNG application took place 
on January 10, 2024,5 at the Farmington Library in Farmington, Connecticut, with around 
40 people attending.6  Nine attendees provided testimony to the Authority, and none 
supported the requested rate increase.  CNG Hr’g Tr., Jan 10, 2024, 2:1–10.  The Mayor 
of Farmington, Joseph Capodiferro, attended and highlighted the impact on average

At the virtual public comment hearing on February 16, 2024, 17 individuals 
provided testimony to the Authority.  CNG Hr’g Tr., Feb. 16, 2024, 2:11–20.  Of those, four 
speakers specifically addressed CNG, all opposing the proposed rate increase.  Their 
objections included concerns about the impact on vulnerable ratepayers, such as small 
and minority-owned businesses, and a desire for the state to reduce its reliance on fossil 
fuels like natural gas.  Additionally, five people, without specifying affiliation to either CNG 
or SCG, also opposed the rate increase, emphasizing the need for the state to transition 
from fossil fuels to greener energy sources. 
Through the close of the evidentiary record on May 29, 2024, the Authority 
received a total of 39 letters and emails related specifically to CNG.  Three of those letters 
authored specifically regarding CNG supported the proposed application.  The primary 
concerns expressed by the letters and emails in opposition were the negative financial 
impact on customers, particularly senior citizens, and low-income families.  Given the 
current cost of living and inflation, the requested increase would place additional financial 
strain on customers.  This sentiment was echoed by the Executive Director of the North 
Hartford Partnership (NHP), which is focused on community revitalization in areas such 
as housing, economic development, public safety, health, and education.  NHP Corresp., 
Feb. 16, 2024, p. 1.  The NHP's letter argued that the rate increase would further harm 
residents and commercial ratepayers, including small and minority-owned businesses.  
Id., p. 2.  Additionally, AARP submitted its concerns regarding the combined rate case of 
CNG and SCG on behalf of its members in Connecticut, particularly those aged 50 and 
over on fixed or low incomes who struggle in the current inflationary environment.  AARP 
Corresp., Nov. 29, 2023, p. 2.  AARP opposes increases, including increases to monthly 
fixed charges, because they make controlling gas spending harder and discourage 
conservation.  Id., pp. 2–3. 
A significant number of comments were received during this proceeding, with many 
addressing both CNG and SCG or being non-specific to either company.  The largest 
portion consisted of 168 written comments opposing the requested rate increase.  These 
comments primarily focused on climate issues, urging the Authority to reject the 
application, and emphasizing the need for the state to align its investments with current 
climate laws and to reduce its reliance on fracked gas.  EOE Brief, p. 40. 
Conversely, the Authority received comments that support the rate increase 
application.  Among the supportive comments was a letter from the Mayor of East 
Hartford, Connor Martin, which urged the Authority to approve the application.  The mayor 
highlighted that the approval would enhance safety by replacing aging infrastructure and 
benefit the environment by reducing the release of greenhouse gases (GHG).  Martin 
Corresp., April 15, 2024.

II. 
STANDARD OF REVIEW 
The Authority is statutorily charged with regulating the rates of Connecticut’s public 
service companies.  General Statutes § 16-19.  The term “public service company” is 
defined to include gas companies, such as CNG.  General Statutes § 16-1.  Consequently, 
CNG must “file any proposed amendment of its existing rates with the [A]uthority in such 
form and in accordance with such reasonable regulations as the [A]uthority may 
prescribe.”8  General Statutes § 16-19(a).  Once a proposed rate amendment has been 
filed, the Authority is responsible for making “such investigation of such proposed 
amendment of rates as is necessary to determine whether such rates conform to the 
principles and guidelines” in General Statutes § 16-19e, and the Authority must 
investigate whether the rates “are unreasonably discriminatory or more or less than just, 
reasonable and adequate, or that the service furnished by such company is inadequate 
to or in excess of public necessity and convenience . . . .”  General Statutes § 16-19(a). 
Importantly, a public service company bears “the burden of proving the proposed 
rate under consideration is just and reasonable.”  General Statutes § 16-22.  In placing 
the burden on the company in rate cases, the General Assembly has attempted to remedy 
a critical challenge in setting rates — asymmetric access to information.  The utility 
maintains most of the relevant and critical information necessary for the Authority to make

findings of fact and associated determinations on rates.  Therefore, the Authority and 
other parties are at an information disadvantage compared to the utility and must rely on 
the utility’s application materials, the utility’s responses to interrogatories, and the utility’s 
witness testimony.  Accordingly, the burden of proof established by General Statutes § 
16-22 addresses the information imbalance by imposing an affirmative obligation on the 
utility to present sufficient evidence to support its proposed rate amendment. 
In administrative proceedings, which are subject to the provisions of the Uniform 
Administrative Procedures Act (UAPA), General Statutes § 4-166 et seq., the appropriate 
standard of proof is the preponderance of the evidence.  See Jones v. Connecticut 
Medical Examining Board, 309 Conn. 727, 734–35, 741 n.7 (2013) (“default rule is the 
preponderance of the evidence standard in the absence of legislation to the contrary”); 
Goldstar Medical Services, Inc. v. Dept. of Social Services, 288 Conn. 790, 821 (2008) 
(same).  “That burden of proof is met when [the company] shows the facts supporting [its] 
case are found to be more probable than not.”  Connecticut Light & Power Co. v. 
Connecticut Dept. of Public Utility Control, No. CV094019951S, 2010 WL 797137, at *10 
(Conn. Super. Ct. Feb. 5, 2010) (citing Tianti v. William Raveis Real Estate, Inc., 231 
Conn. 690, 702 (1995)).  Consequently, to carry its statutory burden, the utility must 
provide (or ensure the record contains) evidence that, inter alia, the requested rates are 
consistent with the principles that rates be “sufficient, but no more than sufficient,” General 
Statutes § 16-19e(a)(4), and “reflect prudent and efficient management.”  General 
Statutes § 16-19e(a)(5). 
Notably, the utility bears the burden of providing more than mere declarations of 
fact.  Connecticut Natural Gas Corp. v. Public Utilities Commission, 29 Conn. Supp. 379, 
394 (1971) (finding “no sacrosanctity about the testimony of any company officer 
regardless of his position which gives such testimony any godlike fiat that must be 
accepted out of hand” by the Authority).  “Bald statements need to be covered with some 
evidential hair” before they are acceptable.  Id.  Further, “[a]n administrative agency is not 
required to believe any witness, even an expert.”  Goldstar, 288 Conn. at 830.  It is the 
province of the trier of fact, in this case, the Authority, to “make determinations of 
credibility, crediting some, all, or none of a given witness’ testimony.”  Id. 
The Authority’s review of the proposed rates is guided, in part, by the principle “that 
the level and structure of rates be sufficient, but no more than sufficient, to allow public 
service companies to cover their operating and capital costs, to attract needed capital 
and to maintain their financial integrity, and yet provide appropriate protection to the 
relevant public interests, both existing and foreseeable.”  General Statutes § 16-19e(a)(4).  
That language “tracks, almost verbatim, the language that the United States Supreme 
Court used in Hope when it interpreted the ‘just and reasonable’ requirement under the 
Natural Gas Act and the federal constitution.”  Connecticut Light & Power Co. v. Dept. of 
Public Utility Control, 216 Conn. 627, 635 (1990) (referencing Federal Power Commission 
v. Hope Natural Gas Co., 320 U.S. 591, 603 (1944)).  A regulated utility is entitled to an 
opportunity to recover prudent operating expenses as well as capital costs, including a 
fair and reasonable rate of return on capital investments.  See Federal Power 
Commission v. Hope Natural Gas Co., 320 U.S. at 603; Bluefield Waterworks &

Improvement Co. v. Public Service Commission of West Virginia, 262 U.S. 679, 690 
(1923) (company entitled to ask for fair return upon value of capital employed for public 
convenience); see also Duquesne Light Co. v. Barasch, 488 U.S. 299, 310 (1989) 
(affirming the holding in Hope that “[i]f the total effect of the rate order cannot be said to 
be unreasonable, judicial inquiry . . . is at an end.”).  “The prudence of a management 
decision depends on good faith and reasonableness, judged at the time the decision is 
made.”  Connecticut Light & Power Co. v. Dept. of Public Utility Control, 216 Conn. at 
645. 
Ultimately, however, rate setting requires “a balancing of the investor and 
consumer interests.”  Woodbury Water Co. v. Public Utilities Commission, 174 Conn. 258, 
264 (1978) (quoting Federal Power Commission v. Hope Natural Gas Co., 320 U.S. at 
603).  Further, the constitution does not bind the Authority “to the use of any single formula 
or combination of formulae in determining rates,” and the ratemaking process may involve 
“pragmatic adjustments.”  Woodbury Water Co. v. Public Utilities Commission, 174 Conn. 
at 264 (1978) (quoting Federal Power Commission v. Natural Gas Pipeline Co., 315 U.S. 
575, 586 (1942)).  In striking this balance and making pragmatic adjustments, the 
Authority is guided by the principles of General Statutes § 16-19e(a), noted above. 
III. 
TEST YEAR 
A test year “is employed to show what the probable operating and financial 
condition of the company will be in the immediate future, in order that rates may be fixed 
which will compensate the company for all operating expenses and provide it with a fair 
return.”  Southern New England Telephone Co. v. Public Utilities Commission, 29 Conn. 
Supp. 253, 258 (1970).  The test year in each rate application must “consist of the most 
recent twelve-month period available ending at a calendar quarter.”  Conn. Agencies 
Regs. § 16-1-54.  Test year financial data is “limited to the actual income and expenses 
as determined on the accrual basis during the subject period without adjustment or 
alteration.”  Id.  Applicants are required to present financial data through the SFRs.  See 
Conn. Agencies Regs. § 16-1-53. 
Here, CNG proposed the period beginning January 1, 2022, and ending on 
December 31, 2022, as the test year (Test Year).  Application, p. 2. 
IV. 
RATE BASE 
A. 
SUMMARY 
Rate base is a fundamental principle of cost-of-service ratemaking.  Rate base is 
the investor-supplied facilities and other investments necessary to supply a utility service 
to consumers in a safe, reliable, and cost-effective manner.  For purposes of ratemaking, 
rate base is the capital on which the investor may earn a return.  See Bluefield Waterworks 
& Improvement Co. v. Public Service Commission of West Virginia, 262 U.S. at 690 (a 
“company is entitled to ask [for] a fair return upon the value of that which it employs for 
the public convenience.”).

Docket No. 23-11-02 
Page 9 
 
 
 
Cost-of-service ratemaking provides a return on rate base, which is the capital that 
has been prudently invested by shareholders and put to public use.  Id.  Consequently, 
determining rate base requires a two-prong assessment.  First, the utility must prove that 
the company’s plant is in use and is serving the public.  See Cedar Island Improvement 
Association. v. Clinton Electric Light & Power Co., 142 Conn. 359, 370 (1955) (“public 
utility company is entitled to a fair return upon the fair value of such of its property as is 
useful and being used in providing service”).  Second, the company must prove that the 
capital investment was prudent and reasonable.  See General Statutes § 16-19e(a)(5) 
(“the level and structure of rates charged customers shall reflect prudent and efficient 
management”). 
The “used and useful” standard is a “bedrock principle of utility regulation.”  
Kentucky Utilities Co. v. Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, 760 F.2d 1321, 1324 
n.4 (D.C. Cir. 1985).  “Generally speaking, property not employed in the public service 
should not be incorporated into the base to be used to compute the fair rate of return.  It 
must be kept in mind, however, that whether utility property is used or useful for inclusion 
in the rate base is a factual determination rather than a legal question.”  Southern New 
England Telephone Co. v. Public Utilities Commission, 29 Conn. Supp. 253, 259–60 
(1970).  The Authority does not allow for the inclusion of incomplete system additions or 
improvements into a company’s pro forma rate base.  See, e.g., Decision, May 19, 2021, 
Docket No. 20-10-31, Application of Jewett City Water Company to Amend its Rate 
Schedules, p. 23.  “[R]atepayers benefit from the plant additions when they are in-service 
and . . . ratepayers should not be responsible for providing a return on plant that is not in-
service.”).  Id., p. 24. 
Once a company has proven that property is used and useful, it must also establish 
that the capital investment was prudent and reasonable.  See General Statutes § 16-
19e(a)(5).  Specifically, “there exists a distinction between, on one hand, utility property 
and, on the other hand, the cost of utility property allowed in rate base, because only that 
portion of utility property that is the result of prudent and reasonable management is 
included in rate base.”  Connecticut Light & Power Co. v. Dept. of Public Utility Control, 
219 Conn. 61, 68 (1991).  To demonstrate prudency, the utility must provide evidence that 
the decision to undertake the investment was reasonable at the time it was made and 
that the capital project was managed in a reasonable and cost-effective manner.  In sum, 
to establish its rate base for ratemaking purposes, the Company must demonstrate, by a 
preponderance of the evidence, that the capital proposed for inclusion in rate base (1) is 
used and useful and (2) was invested prudently. 
Rate base is calculated by taking the test year net book value of prudent capital 
investments and accounting for other factors, including accumulated depreciation, 
working capital, and non-rate base capital such as deferred taxes.  The test year is 
intended to “be representative of conditions which will probably prevail in the immediate 
future when the rates will be effective.”  Connecticut Natural Gas Corp. v. Public Utilities 
Commission, 29 Conn. Supp. at 390.  Certain pro forma adjustments may be permitted 
to recognize capital investments and other changes to rate base that occur subsequent 
to the test year.  Id., p. 390 (“company should be permitted to adjust the test year forward

2. Audit Procedure 
To investigate the reasonableness of the capital additions proposed by CNG, 
PURA staff conducted audits at the Company’s headquarters.  The audits were aimed at 
promoting transparency, verifying responsible decision-making, and validating the 
legitimacy of project expenditures. 
A critical component of the audit involved comparing the $891,543,166 plant-in-
service balance from the Company’s previous rate case with the current $1,419,837,010 
request.  Late Filed Ex. 1, Att. 2, Sch. B-1.0; Late Filed Ex. 1, Att. 3; Interrog. Resp. RRU-
443, p. 2; Interrog. Resp. RRU-443, Att. 1; Interrog. Resp. RRU-443, Supp. Att. 1.  This 
comparison aims to safeguard ratepayer interests by ensuring that all incremental capital 
investments being sought for recovery in rate base were fully disclosed and accounted 
for.  Concurrently, PURA Staff examined the Company's procurement policies and 
practices to assess whether they reflect prudent and efficient management.   See General 
Statutes § 16-19e(a)(5).  Another key aspect of the audit was the evaluation of alternative 
analyses presented by the Company for various projects.  Specifically, PURA Staff 
evaluated different project execution decisions to assess whether they were cost effective 
and aligned with the best interests of ratepayers. 
To further investigate the legitimacy of project expenditures, PURA Staff also 
conducted an in-depth review of invoices and supporting documentation provided by the 
Company.  This examination aimed to verify that claimed costs were accurate, 
reasonable, and directly related to the capital additions under review.

c. Underutilized Mains and Service Lines 
The Company seeks recovery for certain gas mains and service lines that are not 
serving meters and are, therefore, unutilized or underutilized.  Specifically, the Company 
requests recovery for mains “for which no service or meter currently actively serves 
customers.”  Interrog. Resp. RRU-766 Supp. (May 29, 2024), p. 3.  The Company argues 
that these assets are used and useful because they are “energized, as at that time they 
become capable of serving a customer or providing pressure delivery support of . . . the 
distribution system.”  Id.  The Company also claims that the mains are used and useful 
because they are capitalized consistent with Generally Accepted Accounting Principles 
(GAAP) and the FERC Uniform System of Accounts.  CNG Hr’g Tr., May 22, 2024, 
1825:14–18.  Here, the Authority will permit the incorporation of the underutilized mains 
and service lines into rate base (both through the Test Year and Pro Forma additions).  
However, because this plant was installed for purposes of generating revenue from 
customers and that revenue has not materialized, the Authority finds it appropriate to 
implement an ROE adjustment to properly incentivize the Company with respect to 
securing business revenue.  Importantly, due to revenue decoupling, existing ratepayers 
must compensate the Company for the lost revenue resulting from underutilized mains 
and service lines.  Essentially, the Company is indemnified for its decision to install plant 
that ultimately produces little or no revenue.  Consequently, to align the Company’s 
interests with that of ratepayers, the Authority will reduce the Company’s ROE to ensure 
the Company is properly incentivized to reduce lost revenue and to fully utilize the mains 
and service lines, for which ratepayers are paying.

customers served by this plant.  Importantly, the evidence in this record indicates that the

by 5 basis points to encourage efficient management and reduction of underutilized plant.  
This reduction accounts for only a portion of the increase in the revenue requirement for 
this plant.  In the Company’s next rate case, the Authority will review the Company’s 
efforts to minimize underutilized plant and determine if continued action is required.  The 
Company projects in its five-year capital plan that it will spend approximately $10,000,000 
per year for new business.  Application, Sch. F-7.0; Late Filed Ex. 1, Att. 2 Rev., Sch F.-
7.0.  To reduce the risk of ratepayer subsidization of underutilized plant while 
accommodating circumstances that may be outside the Company’s control, the amount 
of underutilized plant should account for less than 5% of those annual investments 
(~$500,000 per year).  Although the actual amount of acceptable underutilization will 
depend on the facts, the 5% target is a reasonable starting point in light of the 
approximately $2.8 million of underutilized plant being added to rate base in this

During the proceeding, the question arose as to whether plant that has not yet 
been through the Company’s internal review and approval process is eligible for recovery 
in rate base.  Specifically, OCC argues that certain 2024 plant additions made by the 
Company should be disallowed because the Company’s “internal budgetary approval

The Company asserts that OCC’s conclusion and recommendation is “flawed and 
based on several misconceptions of the Companies’ internal approval process and plant 
additions exhibits.”  Application, CNG Reply Brief, p. 28.  The Company further asserts 
that the projects in question are “primarily long-established annual programs where the 
discrete projects are significantly below the $1,000,000 threshold for [sic] and executed 
on work orders.”  Id., p. 30.  The Company further states that “although the overall 
program funding is approved by the [Investment Review Group (IRG)], the projects within 
the program are authorized to proceed based upon approvals of the individual work 
orders.”  Id., p. 30.  The Company additionally notes that the items requested for IRG 
review “are for capital expenditures, most of which are [Construction Work in Progress

Depreciation, in this context, refers to the loss in value “in connection with the 
consumption or prospective retirement of utility plant in the course of service from causes 
which are known to be in current operation and against which the utility is not protected 
by insurance.”  Dunkel Prefiled Test., Feb. 8, 2023, p. 4 (quoting the FERC Uniform 
System of Accounts prescribed for Natural Gas Companies Subject to the Provisions of 
the Natural Gas Act).  Depreciation accounts for “wear and tear, decay, action of the 
elements, inadequacy, obsolescence, changes in the art, changes in demand and 
requirements of public authorities, and, in the case of natural gas companies, the 
exhaustion of natural resources.”  Id.  Depreciation expense is credited to the Company’s 
depreciation reserve account (also known as accumulated depreciation) and 
accumulates there until the plant actually retires.  Id., p. 22.  When the plant does retire, 
the net salvage cost is paid out of the depreciation reserve.  Id. 
Accumulated depreciation (or depreciation reserve) reflects the amount of 
depreciation expense that has been allowed in rates and accumulated to date, less any 
retirements and net salvage received as an offset to rate base.  See Decision, July 28, 
2021, Docket No. 20-12-30, Application of the Connecticut Water Company to Amend its 
Rate Schedule (2021 CWC Rate Case Decision), p. 70.  As such, the depreciation reserve 
reflects the asset deterioration of in-service plant and is maintained in anticipation of 
future asset replacement or retirement needs.  Id.  The accumulated depreciation should 
be based on the depreciation rates and useful service lives that fall within the National 
Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners (NARUC) guidelines and have been 
allowed or approved by the Authority.  Id.  Ideally, assets are depreciated consistently, 
i.e., proportionally, with the rate of the actual deterioration of assets until they are retired 
or replaced.  Id. 
A depreciation rate study proposes annual depreciation rates to be applied to plant-
in-service balances.  The product of the depreciation rate and plant-in-service balance is 
the annual depreciation expense, which is recorded to reflect the annual recovery or 
amortization of previously expended capital investment.  The depreciation expense 
impacts the calculation of accumulated depreciation as any depreciation expense allowed

b. Lead/Lag Study 
For larger utilities, the Authority has established a preference that a lead/lag study 
be conducted to determine the appropriate CWC allowance, rather than rely on a heuristic 
approach (such as a percentage of an operation and maintenance (O&M) expense).  In 
this proceeding, CNG conducted a lead/lag study and requests that the results of that 
study be used for determining the CWC component of its Rate Year rate base.  Lead-Lag 
Study and Cash Working Capital Panel PFT, p. 3.  The Company's study detailed the 
timing of expenses and revenues.  Id., p. 4.  The study calculated a revenue "lag" 
(measured in days), which was the Company’s calculation of the number of days between 
when the Company provided service and when the customer paid for that service.  Id.  
The study also calculated an expense “lead” (also measured in days), which represented 
the Company’s calculation of the number of days between when the Company incurred 
an expense and when it paid for the expense.  Id.  The net of the revenue lag days and 
expense lead days provided a net lag that the Company then multiplied by the Company’s 
average daily rate year expense to calculate the Company’s proposed CWC.  Lead-Lag

In its calculation of CWC, the Company included non-cash items, such as

CWC calculation.  Defever Revised Prefiled Test., Apr. 19, 2024, p. 6. 
The Company notes that there are two “commonly used” methodologies for 
calculating CWC that are used by regulated utilities.  Lead-Lag Study and Cash Working

approach” (Approach 1), which does not include non-cash items, but “considers all cash 
flows, including typical cash expenses such as compensation, benefits, regulatory 
assessments, taxes, and interest expense.”  Id., p. 5.  The Company refers to the other 
methodology as the “non-O&M approach” (Approach 2), which uses all cash flows but

retained net income.”  Id., p. 5.  The Company uses this second methodology.  Id.  The

Included in the Company’s $9,119,522 in deferred expenses are carrying charges, 
which are not permissible on deferred expenses without explicit prior Authority approval.  
First, under Accounting Standards Codification (Accounting Standards) 980-340-25-1, an 
accounting regulatory asset is limited to “an incurred costs that would otherwise be 
charged to expense.”  Importantly, the Financial Accounting Standards Board, which 
established GAAP, distinguishes between “incurred cost” and “allowable cost.”  See 
Accounting Standards 980-10-20.  Incurred cost is “a cost arising from cash paid out or 
obligation to pay for an acquired asset or service, a loss from any cause that has been 
sustained and must be paid for.”  Id.  By contrast, an allowable cost is “all costs for which 
revenue is intended to provide recovery” and can “include interest costs and amounts 
provided for earnings on shareholders’ investments.”  Id.  Carrying charges are not 
assets, services, or losses that must be “paid for”; therefore, they are not “incurred costs 
that would otherwise be charged to expense.”  As such, an accounting regulatory asset 
recognized by the Company under GAAP is limited to the specific expenses that were 
paid for by the utility and authorized for deferred accounting.  Any other costs, including 
carrying charges, are allowable costs subject to the Authority’s determination of recovery 
in a rate proceeding. 
Second, allowing carrying charges to accrue on deferred expenses that have not 
been subject to scrutiny and a prudency review is inconsistent with general ratemaking 
principles.  The regulatory asset is already an extraordinary form of relief for utilities as it 
permits recovery of certain expenses beyond the base distribution revenue requirement 
authorized at the time the expense was incurred.  Stated another way, regulatory assets 
allow recovery of expenses that otherwise would be borne entirely by the utility.  
Therefore, expanding the deferred accounting beyond the actual “incurred costs” prior to 
a full prudency review and determination of recovery is applying extraordinary relief upon 
extraordinary relief.  Moreover, enabling the collection of carrying charges on deferred 
expenses prior to a prudency review may incent a delay, perhaps indefinitely, in the

PROXY GROUP 
The Authority identified a group of six companies (Authority Proxy Group) to 
ascertain the market-based range of the cost of equity (COE) for the Company.  The 
Authority uses certain criteria (Authority Screening Criteria) to identify companies that 
have a similar risk and investment profile as the Company.  Generally, a company will be 
considered a proxy company if it: 
(1) derives at least 70% of revenue from regulated utilities, as reported by Value Line; 
(2) derives at least 50% of regulated revenue from regulated gas distribution, as 
reported by Value Line; 
(3) is publicly traded and reported by Value Line;  
(4) has paid consistent dividends for eight quarters and is expected to continue; 
(5) is not in financial distress; 
(6) is not the target of an acquisition or merger activity; 
(7) has credit ratings that are at least investment grade, as determined by S&P 
Global (BBB- and above) and/or Moody’s Investor Service (Moody’s) (Baa3 
and above); and 
(8) is not projected to have negative earnings growth as reported by Value Line.

3. Capital Structure Analysis 
The Authority establishes the ratemaking capital structure by carefully weighing 
several factors, including: the actual capital structure of the utility and its parent company, 
the range of capital structures of the proxy group, and the credit rating agency metrics.  
The Authority is obligated to balance both investor and consumer interests in reaching a 
determination on the appropriate capital structure.  Woodbury Water Co., 174 Conn. at 
264.  Generally, the utility will advocate for a higher equity component in its capital 
structure because a higher equity component generally provides a higher return for its 
investors.  At the same time, a higher equity component also decreases the financial risk 
of the Company as it holds less debt in its capital structure.  Conversely, parties such as 
OCC will often advocate for a lower equity component in the Company's capitalization 
structure because debt is generally less expensive for ratepayers than equity. 
However, investor and consumer interests in capital structure are not entirely 
divergent.  Specifically, a capital structure with too little equity could maximize the benefits 
of lower cost debt but would ultimately increase the Company’s risk profile and, hence, 
the cost of equity.  On the other hand, a capital structure with too much equity would 
unnecessarily burden ratepayers with a more expensive capital structure and not achieve

Docket No. 23-11-02 
Page 47 
 
 
 
the lowest cost of capital for the Company that balances both risk and the overall cost of 
capital.  Consequently, the Authority must account for a variety of factors to find an optimal 
capitalization mix for the Company’s cost of capital. 
a. Approved and Actual Capital Structure 
The first factor to consider when determining a reasonable capital structure for 
ratemaking purposes is the approved and actual capital structure of the Company.  In the 
2018 CNG Rate Case Decision, the Authority approved a settlement with an equity 
capitalization of 54% for rate year 1 (2019), 54.50% for rate year 2 (2020), and 55% for 
rate year 3 (2021) for ratemaking purposes.  2018 CNG Rate Case Decision, pp. 7–8, 11.  
Consequently, the Company’s approved equity capitalization since 2019 has ranged from 
54% to 55%.  Interrog. Resp. OCC-6, Att. 1.  The Company has maintained an A rating 
from S&P, an A2 rating from Moody’s, and an A- rating from Fitch with an allowed equity 
capitalization of 55%.  Interrog. Resp. OCC-10, Att. 1, pp. 76, 119; Interrog. Resp. RRU-
398, Att. 3. 
For the period of January 2022 to September 2023, the Company calculated an 
end-of-period average equity capitalization of 58.21%, which is higher than the 
Company’s approved capital structure.  Interrog. Resp. OCC-6, Att. 1.  The Company did 
not provide data regarding its equity capitalization prior to the Test Year (i.e., for 2019, 
2020, or 2021).  As such, it is unclear as to whether the end of period average of 58.21% 
is reflective of the Company’s capital structure since the last rate case or more recent 
financial adjustments made by the parent company.  Notably, the Company’s equity 
capitalization increased fairly sharply starting in 2023.  See Woolridge PFT, Ex. JRW-4, 
p. 2.  Specifically, the Company’s equity capitalization was 55.00% in November 2022 but 
had risen to 61.97% by May 2023.  Id.  This increase of almost 7% over a 6-month period 
indicates that the Company’s end of period average of 58.21% is biased upwards due to 
recent financial activity and not necessarily reflective of an appropriate ratemaking 
capitalization. 
As a result, the Authority finds that the Company’s approved equity capitalization 
and the data related to its actual equity capitalization indicates a range of 54% to 56% 
equity.

companies in the proxy groups, (3) the credit rating agency metrics, and (4) the use of

of 52.6% (subsidiary) and 49.70% (holding company).  Combined with the fact that the 
Company seems to be (recently) operating at an elevated equity capitalization (58.21%), 
the Authority finds a capital structure consisting of 53% common equity, 46.26% long-
term debt, 0.06% preferred equity, and 0.68% short-term debt will permit a reasonably 
optimal cost of capital.  By adopting a capitalization mix with an equity component that is 
at the higher end of the range of the parties’ proxy groups, the Authority seeks to lower 
the Company’s risk profile and, therefore, allow the opportunity to lower the Company’s 
cost of debt component of the overall cost of capital.

1. Summary 
The Authority finds an ROE of 9.15%, as adjusted for a 5 basis point reduction, to 
be reasonable.  In reaching this determination, the Authority considered a variety of 
factors, including widely accepted financial models for calculating commensurate ROEs, 
comparable approved ROEs, current economic and market conditions, and the impact on 
the Company’s creditworthiness. 
2. Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) Financial Model 
a. DCF Model Description 
The DCF model is a market-based financial model that attempts to replicate the 
valuation process used by investors.  The DCF model assumes that investors evaluate 
stocks in a classical economic framework and buy and sell securities rationally at prices 
that reflect the assets’ value.  Under the DCF model, the value of a financial asset is 
based upon the present value principle.  Specifically, the present value of a financial asset 
equals the discounted value of its expected future cash flows.  Investors discount these 
expected cash flows at their required rate of return (i.e., the COE or ROE).  Therefore, by 
using proxy company data, the DCF model provides evidence of commensurate ROEs 
for utilities with corresponding risk profiles. 
The traditional constant growth DCF Model requires the following assumptions: a 
constant growth rate for earnings and dividends; a stable dividend payout ratio; a constant 
price-to-earnings ratio; and a discount rate greater than the expected growth rate.

The DCF model is represented by the formula of K = D1 / Po + G, where: 
K = the market-required ROE; 
D1 = the forecasted dividend paid one period into the future; 
Po = an estimate to the current market price of the stock; and 
G = investors’ long-run growth expectations. 
In short, the ROE (K) can be determined by summing the expected dividend yield 
(D1/Po) and the expected growth rate (G). 
b. Expected Growth Rate 
The Authority first considers the expected growth rate for the companies in the 
Authority Proxy Group because the expected growth rate is also a factor in calculating 
the expected dividend yield.  The constant growth form of the DCF Model assumes a 
single growth estimate in perpetuity.  To reduce the expected growth rate to a single 
measure, the constant payout ratio, EPS, dividends per share (DPS), and book value per 
share (BVPS) are assumed to all grow at the same constant rate.  The distinction between 
the parties’ approaches to the expected growth rate is (1) the specific growth measures 
considered and (2) the weighting of the measures. 
For its expected growth rate, the Company averaged the long-term EPS growth

earned returns on common equity.  Id.  The Company limited its analysis to EPS growth

c. Expected Dividend Yield 
The second input into the DCF model is the Expected Dividend Yield.  For 
purposes of the DCF model, the Expected Dividend Yield is estimated by taking a 
company’s current annual dividend yield and escalating the yield to account for 
anticipated growth and the timing of dividends. 
A company’s current dividend yield is not subject to much dispute because a 
company’s dividend and stock price are both published market data.  To avoid transient 
stock price anomalies, an average daily stock price is typically used, with the time period 
ranging from 30 to 180 trading days.  Here, as has been found in other recent rate cases, 
the Authority finds a 30-trading day average stock price to be appropriate, because it 
represents the most current pricing data over a reasonable duration of time and, in this 
case, the 30-day time frame does not reflect any significant market disruptions that might 
unreasonably impact the average stock price.  See 2024 CWC Rate Case Decision, p.

3. Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) 
a. CAPM Model Description 
The CAPM evaluates the relationship between the expected return and risk of 
investing in a security and can be used to calculate the expected return of an asset.  
Therefore, like the DCF model, by incorporating proxy company data, the CAPM provides 
evidence of commensurate ROEs for utilities with corresponding risk profiles.  To 
determine the COE, the CAPM first determines the appropriate risk-free rate and then 
adds a beta, or the degree of co-movement of the security’s rate of return with the 
market’s rate of return, multiplied by the expected equity risk premium (ERP), which is 
the amount by which investors expect the future return on equities, in general, to exceed 
that on the risk-free asset. 
The CAPM model is represented by the formula Ke = Rf + β (Rm-Rf), where: 
Ke= the required market ROE; 
β = Beta coefficient of an individual security; 
Rf = the risk-free rate of return; and  
Rm = the required return on the market; the term (Rm - Rf) represents the ERP.  
Consequently, once the Beta (β) and ERP (Rm- Rf) are determined, an ROE can 
be calculated.

4. Empirical Capital Asset Pricing Model 
The Company also included the results of an empirical capital asset pricing model 
(ECAPM).  Cost of Capital Panel PFT, p. 43.  The ECAPM calculates the product of an 
adjusted beta coefficient and market risk premium by applying a weight of 0.25 to the 
market risk premium and 0.75 to the result.  Id., pp. 43–44.  The Company’s ECAPM 
formula is represented by: Ke = Rf + 0.75 β(Rm – Rf) + 0.25(Rm – Rf); where: Ke is the 
required market ROE; β is the Adjusted Beta coefficient of an individual security; Rf is the 
risk-free rate of return; and Rm is the required return on the market as a whole.  Id.  The 
Company’s ECAPM analysis results in a range of ROE returns from 10.89% to 11.53%.  
Id., p. 44; Cost of Capital Panel PFT, Ex. CNG-AEB-5. 
OCC indicated that the ECAPM has not been theoretically or empirically validated 
in journals.  Woolridge PFT, p. 80.  Beyond the lack of validation, ECAPM has two main 
flaws: (1) there are no known tests of the CAPM that use adjusted betas as posed by the 
Company; and (2) using adjusted betas addresses the empirical issues with CAPM.  Id. 
The Authority has previously reviewed the ECAPM approach and excluded this 
method.  See 2024 CWC Rate Case Decision, p. 57; 2023 UI Rate Case Decision, pp. 
84–85; 2018 CNG Rate Case Decision, pp. 40–41.  Here, the Authority reviewed the 
proposed ECAPM and sees no difference from past submissions.  The most recent 
rationale for rejection of the ECAPM holds true today: the Authority finds that the 0.75/0.25 
factor is out-of-date (based on 30 plus year old data) and incorporates another level of 
conjecture that is unnecessary given that the simple CAPM formula is widely accepted in 
COE literature.  Second, given that ECAPM is only discussed within the regulatory cost 
of capital sphere, ECAPM has not been theoretically or empirically validated in financial 
journals.  Third, the purpose of adjusted betas, such as those from Value Line and 
Bloomberg, addresses the empirical issues with the CAPM; hence, there is no need for 
an additional adjustment factor to adjust for what is being addressed by using Value Line 
and Bloomberg betas.  The Authority reaffirms its rejection of ECAPM and will not give 
evidentiary weight to the data.

6. Current Economic Conditions 
The Authority reviewed changes to certain financial indicators comparing current 
yields to those present at the 2018 CNG Rate Case Decision.  The purpose of this static 
analysis is to provide a barometer to establish the direction in ROE as compared to the 
prior authorized ROE.  In addition to trends in economic conditions, the Authority also 
relies on its COE models to establish the ultimate allowed ROE. 
To assess current economic conditions, the Authority reviewed several indicators.  
For example, since January 1, 2021, through the last quarter of 2023, US Gross Domestic 
Product (GDP) increased from 107.73 to 123.29, or by 14.44%, and the Consumer Price 
Index (CPI) increased from 261.58 to 306.75, or 17.26%, while national unemployment 
decreased by from 6.40% to 3.70% over that period.  Interrog. Resp. RRU-540, Att. 1. 
Interest rates have also increased since January 2021, but the increase in interest 
rates was greater at the short end of the yield curve (i.e., 90- and 180-day US Treasury 
Bills) as compared to the long-end (i.e., UST 20-year and UST 30-year year).  Id.  For 
example, 90-day and 180-day US Treasury Bills were 0.08% and 0.09%, respectively, in 
January 2021, and as of the end of 2023, stood at 5.44% and 5.34%, respectively.  Id.  
US Treasury Bonds of 10-year, 20-year, and 30-year maturities were at 1.08%, 1.63%, 
and 1.82%, respectively, in January 2021, and as of the end of 2023, US Treasury Bonds 
of 10-year, 20-year, and 30-year maturities were at 4.02%, 4.32%, and 4.14%, 
respectively.  Id.  Investor inflation expectations as measured by inflation-projected 
Treasuries known as TIPS have fallen off since mid-2022 and are now at an expected 
inflation rate of 2.25% over the next five years.  Woolridge PFT, pp. 12–13.  The expected 
inflation rates over the next ten and thirty years are 2.30% and 2.20%, respectively.  Id.  
OCC’s witness surmised that the expected long-term inflation rate is around 2.25%.  Id. 
Although inflation has moved interest rates up over the past year, OCC does not 
believe that interest rates will increase in 2024.  Woolridge PFT, pp. 13–15.  The OCC 
witness described the yield curve, which is usually upward sloping because investors 
require higher returns to commit capital for longer periods of time.  Id., pp. 13–14.  The 
yield curve is currently “inverted,” which means that yields on shorter-term maturity 
securities are higher than yields on longer-term securities.  Id., p. 14.  This has typically 
preceded two outcomes according to OCC; the first is that investors do not expect interest 
rates to remain where they are and expect them to decline, and second, the inverted yield 
curve is an indicator of a pending recession, which would also put downward pressure on 
rates.  Id.  OCC indicated that over the last 50 years, every time the yield curve inverted, 
a recession followed.  Woolridge PFT, p. 14.  Given that the market is currently 
demonstrating an inverted yield curve, a recession and lower interest rates are likely to 
follow.  Id., p. 15.

8. Approved ROE 
In determining a reasonable ROE, the Authority considers the analytical models 
for commensurate utility returns, allowed ROEs in other jurisdictions, the prevailing 
market conditions, and the Company’s risk profile.  The Authority considers the two 
analytical models (DCF and CAPM) to provide a target range for commensurate ROEs.  
The Authority generally weighs the DCF model results more heavily than the CAPM 
results because the DCF model relies on directly observable proxy company market data 
and provides a better measure of the COE for similarly situated utilities.  Conversely, the 
CAPM relies primarily on risk-premium studies and market predictions, which are more 
subjective in nature. 
Here, the DCF model as applied to the Authority Proxy Group indicates an ROE 
range of 8.57% to 10.29%, with an average of 9.44%.  The CAPM model produced an 
ROE range of 7.65% to 9.35%, with an average of 8.50%.  Given the Authority’s weighting 
of these models, the data indicates that an ROE between 8.5% and 10.0% would be 
sufficient to provide a reasonable, market-based return. 
Given this range, the Authority must determine an ROE such that the Company 
has an opportunity to “cover . . . [its] capital costs, to attract needed capital and to maintain 
[its] financial integrity.”  General Statutes § 16-19e(a)(4).  This statutory standard reflects 
the long-standing principle that “the return to the equity owner should be commensurate 
with returns on investments in other enterprises having corresponding risks and should 
also be sufficient to assure confidence in the financial integrity of the enterprise, so as to 
maintain its credit and to attract capital.”  Connecticut Light & Power Co. v. Dept. of Public 
Utility Control, 216 Conn. at 634–35.  In determining an ROE, the Authority “is not bound 
to the use of any single formula or combination of formulae” but again must balance 
“investor and consumer interests” and make “pragmatic adjustments.”  Woodbury Water 
Co., 174 Conn. at 264. 
Cognizant of this legal framework, the Authority has analyzed a wide array of 
considerations in reaching a determination, including, without limitation, the Company’s 
capital structure, its financial condition, ROEs from other jurisdictions, analytical models 
of commensurate returns, prevailing and anticipated market conditions, risk factors, and 
the regulatory environment. 
The Company is financially stable, maintaining an A Rating from S&P, an A2 rating 
from Moody’s, and an A- rating from Fitch.  In addition, the Company operates in a 
regulatory environment that reduces risk through the Distribution Integrity Management 
Program (DIMP) mechanism and the revenue decoupling adjustment.  Considering these 
and other factors, the Authority adopts a 9.20% ROE.  Accounting for the 5 basis point 
reduction, the Authority approves a 9.15% ROE.

the franchise operation.”  General Statutes § 16-19e(a)(5).  Therefore, those expenses

6078177-S, 2024 WL 1403433, at *9 (Conn. Super. Ct. Mar. 25, 2024) (application of 
known and measurable standard for depreciation within PURA’s regulatory discretion).  
Consequently, the Authority will consider reasonable historical test year expenses, as 
adjusted for known and measurable changes, to determine a utility's allowable expenses.

The practice of using inflation indices to escalate Test Year expenses is not an 
alternative to the “known and measurable” standard for pro forma adjustments.  Applying 
a broad index inflation factor to specific Test Year expenses is an imprecise methodology 
and not necessarily predictive of the Company’s actual Rate Year costs.  Further, as 
demonstrated by the Company’s selective application of an inflation adjustment, this 
methodology allows a utility to cherry-pick which expenses are escalated by inflation and 
which are escalated by other known and measurable changes.64  With a utility 
incentivized to project higher expenses, this methodology likely results in broad-based 
inflation serving as the floor for expense escalation, thereby creating further upward 
pressure on rates.

circumstances, the application of broad index inflation to a significant portion of Test Year 
expenses is a departure from more targeted applications allowed previously.65

Specifically, inflation escalation permits the utility to, in a way, circumvent its burden to 
demonstrate that pro forma changes are known and measurable.  Evaluating and 
determining known and measurable changes to Test Year expenses can be a tedious 
process, but that process is a fundamental component of ratemaking and a reasonable, 
if not perfect, proxy for free market competition in a monopolized sector.  Consequently, 
utilities should apply inflation adjustments judiciously and, importantly, demonstrate why 
inflation is the appropriate adjustment for a particular expense.  In sum, the Authority finds 
that general inflation escalation is not a substitute for known and measurable changes 
and is, therefore, an improper pro forma adjustment, absent an evidentiary showing that 
escalation is the only reasonable method to determine a Rate Year expense. 
Here, the Company seeks to apply general inflation escalation of 8.31% to a 
substantial portion of its total O&M expenses.  Notably, the Company proposes inflation 
escalation to 36 separate accounts with limited or no explanation as to why inflation is the 
appropriate pro forma adjustment.  See Late Filed Ex. 1, Att. 2.  The Company is 
cautioned against escalating specific costs by an inflation rate without providing an 
evidentiary showing that the rate and its application constitutes a reasonably known and 
measurable change.  If the Company proposes inflation as a pro forma adjustment, the 
Company has the burden of demonstrating that such inflation is a known and measurable 
adjustment to the Test Year expense.  Inflation is not an alternative to a known and 
measurable adjustment; it is an option available to the Company provided the Company 
supports the adjustment with evidence that the Test Year expense has increased or will 
increase by an inflation rate.

ii. Cybersecurity Performance Metrics 
The Authority recognizes the critical importance of cybersecurity in safeguarding 
the Company’s operations and protecting customer data.  To ensure the Company's 
continued improvement in cybersecurity measures, the Authority directs the Company to 
submit proposed cybersecurity-related performance metrics contemporaneous with the 
application in its next rate case.  These metrics should demonstrate the effectiveness of 
the Company's cybersecurity program and its contribution to the overall safety, reliability, 
and resilience of the Company's services.  The metrics should be quantifiable, objective, 
and relevant to the Company’s specific cybersecurity risks and priorities.  The metrics 
should be at the regulated company level and should be industry standard metrics that 
allow for comparison of the Company’s performance to peer utilities or other similar 
organizations.  The Company should seek to leverage existing internal metrics or key 
performance indicators (KPIs); for example, phishing email “click rates.”  The Authority 
encourages the Company to work collaboratively with other stakeholders (including, but 
not limited to, OCC) to identify and develop appropriate cybersecurity performance 
metrics that align with industry best practices and regulatory requirements.

LAUF gas metric is calculated as Gas Distribution System Input (in MCFs) less

5. Gas Forecast Accuracy Metric:  The Company shall measure the variance

calendar year.  The gas forecast accuracy metric is calculated as forecasted Gas 
Distribution System Throughput (in MCFs) less actual Gas Distribution System 
Throughput (in MCFs) divided by actual Gas Distribution System Throughput (in 
MCFs).  Any forecasted vs. actual variance between -5.0% and 5.0% will be 
considered 100% performance achievement.  Any variance in excess of 5.0%, 
positive or negative, between the Company’s forecasted and actual Gas 
Distribution System Throughput will be considered 0% performance achievement.

The Company proposes recovering $2,767,000 in rate case expenses for the 
current proceeding by amortizing the amount over a three-year period, or $922,333 
annually.  Late Filed Ex. 1, Att. 2, Sch. WP C-3.23, p. 1.  The Authority instead permits

To determine whether a utility’s proposed costs are recoverable, the Authority 
conducts a two-step analysis.  First, the Authority must determine whether the costs are 
reflective of prudent and efficient management by the Company.  General Statutes § 16-
19e(a)(5).  To make this determination, the Authority examines the record evidence 
provided by the Company to support the rate case costs.  Such evidence might include 
whether the Company engaged in a competitive solicitation process and compared law 
firms’ and consultants’ hourly rates and the projected number of hours to be spent on the 
rate case proceeding.  The Authority could also consider whether the requested expenses 
are consistent with past rate case cost requests or with the rate case costs in other 
jurisdictions or industry averages.  There is no brightline rule; however, the Company 
must provide sufficient evidence that its incurred costs were prudent. 
Next, after determining the total amount of prudently incurred costs, the Authority 
must balance the interests of ratepayers and the Company in determining just and 
reasonable rates.  Notably, in establishing “the level and structure of rates,” the Authority 
must consider the principles articulated in General Statutes § 16-19e(a), including 
whether “there is a clear public need for the service”, whether costs are necessary “to 
cover [the Company’s] operating costs”, and whether the costs “reflect prudent and 
efficient management of the franchise operation.”  General Statutes §§ 16-19e(a)(1), (4), 
and (5).  To aid in its analysis, the Authority may consider its past practices or practices 
in other jurisdictions.

1. Summary 
A depreciation rate study proposes annual depreciation rates to be applied to plant-
in-service balances.  The product of the depreciation rate and corresponding plant 
balance is the annual depreciation expense, which is a charge to a company’s operating 
expense reflecting the annual recovery or amortization of previously expended capital 
investment.  While depreciation expense is a function of both the depreciation rate and 
the related plant balance, this section focuses only on the Authority's rationale for 
adjusting the Company's proposed depreciation rates.  The Authority’s determinations 
related to the Company’s plant balances are described in Section IV.B, Plant-In-Service. 
Specifically, the Authority will consider: 
(a) Asset Categorization: To simplify the process, the utility categorizes its assets 
(or depreciable plant) based on common characteristics and expected service 
life.  Different asset categories (e.g., mains, services, equipment) will generally 
have unique depreciation rates to reflect the nature of the asset. 
(b) Service Life: The service life of each asset category is based on industry 
standards, historical data, and engineering assessments.  The service life is a 
key component to determining depreciation rates. 
(c) Net Salvage Value: The net salvage value is the gross salvage value of the 
asset less the cost to retire the asset.  In many cases, the net salvage value is 
negative.  The depreciation expense includes a portion of the net salvage 
value. 
(d) Method of depreciation: The most common method used is the straight-line 
depreciation, which spreads the cost of an asset evenly over its useful life. 
To determine the approved depreciation expense, the Authority utilized the Plant 
Model, which calculates depreciation expense by applying the corresponding 
depreciation rates to monthly plant balances.  Specifically, the Authority modified the Plant 
Model to reflect (1) the Authority’s approved plant balances and (2) revised depreciation 
rates.  After incorporating all Authority modifications into the Plant Model, the resulting 
approved Rate Year depreciation expense is $36,791,650.  The Company’s proposed 
Rate Year depreciation expense is $57,156,050. Accordingly, the Authority applies a 
downward adjustment to Rate Year depreciation expense of $20,364,400.

In addition, the Company’s argument that the expired 2017 FCIC is recoverable 
because of a reduced revenue requirement is not persuasive.  First, utilities are generally 
barred from recovering past losses in new rates.  Rate setting is a prospective process 
that prohibits the recovery of past revenue deficiencies or excesses, particularly for a 
single line item — a process known as retroactive or single-issue ratemaking.  Allowing 
the Company to recover this lost revenue in future rates would violate standard 
ratemaking principles.  Notably here, the Company has over-earned in prior years, 
indicating that it may have benefited from either savings or revenues with respect to other 
line items that would not be simultaneously reconciled.

Rate design objectives include: (1) the approval of cost-based, just, and 
reasonable rates that promote further equalization of rates across the Company’s 
divisions; and (2) revenue stability.  See General Statutes § 16-19e(a). 
In striking this balance and making pragmatic adjustments, the Authority is guided 
by General Statutes § 16-19e(a), which states, in relevant part, that the Authority shall 
examine proposed rates in accordance with the following principles: 
(4) that the level and structure of rates be sufficient, but no more than 
sufficient, to allow public service companies to cover their operating costs 
including, but not limited to, appropriate staffing levels, and capital costs, to 
attract needed capital and to maintain their financial integrity, and yet 
provide appropriate protection to the relevant public interests, both existing 
and foreseeable . . .  
(5) that the level and structure of rates charged customers shall reflect 
prudent and efficient management of the franchise operation. 
In furtherance of this statutory framework, the Authority typically employs the rule 
of cost causation, which allocates costs to customers and cost categories based on the 
costs they cause a utility to incur.  The Authority also generally attempts to equalize class 
rates of return, as such practice ensures that rates are not unreasonably discriminatory, 
while balancing the regulatory philosophy of gradualism to, among other reasons, avoid 
customer rate shock.  See J. Lazar et al., Electricity Regulation in the US: A Guide (2d 
Ed. 2016), p. 67, available at: https://www.raponline.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/rap-
lazar-electricity-regulation-US-june-2016.pdf (“sudden large rate changes should be 
avoided where possible to avoid undue new burdens on some classes of customers”).  
Consistent with the philosophy of gradualism, the Authority typically requires rate class 
revenue reductions or increases to be within one and one quarter times the overall 
distribution revenue increase.  See 2016 UI Rate Case Decision, p. 108; see also 2013 
UI Rate Case Decision, p. 153.  Finally, the Authority considers whether “existing or future 
rate structures place an undue burden upon those persons of [low-income] status” as 
contemplated by General Statutes § 16-19e(b).  The Authority weighs the above 
principles and considerations in determining appropriate cost and revenue allocation 
approaches and rate designs.

Currently, the Company benefits from several rate/revenue adjustment

1. Revenue Decoupling Mechanism 
a. Current Revenue Decoupling Mechanism 
The Authority first approved a revenue decoupling mechanism (RDM) to decouple 
the Company’s distribution revenues from the volume of natural gas in the 2013 CNG 
Rate Case.  See 2013 CNG Rate Case Decision, p. 123; General Statutes § 16-19tt.  
Subsequently, the Authority modified the Company’s RDM in CNG’s most recent rate case 
by expanding it to all firm customers, i.e., existing customers and customers on the SE 
Rate, as it previously only applied to non-SE Rate customers.  2018 CNG Rate Case 
Decision, p. 25.  Under the approved RDM, the Company is authorized to perform an 
annual “true up” to reconcile actual revenues to revenues authorized in the Company’s 
previous rate case, collecting additional revenues as necessary to make up for any 
shortfalls in the previous year or conversely, crediting CNG ratepayers if actual revenues 
exceed allowed revenues.  Id.; 2013 CNG Rate Case Decision, pp. 122–123.  In the 2018 
CNG Rate Case Decision, the Authority ordered the Company to submit its RDM filing no 
later than February 25, 2019, and annually thereafter.  Id., p. 41. 
Since 2015, the Company has annually filed an RDM for Authority approval.  The 
Authority last approved the Company’s 2023 RDM filing decoupling surcharge of 
$0.06182474 per ccf to be charged to customers, effective April 1, 2024, through March 
31, 2025.  Motion No. 51 Ruling, Mar. 19, 2024, Docket No. 18-05-16. 
b. Approved RDM 
In any rate case initiated on or after October 23, 2023, the Authority has discretion 
in determining the decoupling mechanism and methodology used in a gas company’s 
decoupling order, subject to the principles set forth in General Statutes § 16-2(m).  
General Statutes § 16-19tt, as amended by Public Act 23-102.  In making such a 
determination, the Authority is required to consider factors, including, but not limited to: 
(1) whether the decoupling mechanism and methodology is in the best interest of 
ratepayers; (2) whether such mechanism and methodology adequately accounts for 
distribution system service outages; and (3) whether such mechanism and methodology 
adequately addresses the disincentive for utilities to engage in conservation and energy 
efficiency measures.  Id.

2. Distribution Integrity Management Program 
a. Overview 
In 2009, the United States Department of Transportation Pipeline and Hazardous 
Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) implemented integrity management regulations 
for natural gas distribution systems, or DIMP regulations, that are intended to help ensure 
pipeline integrity and improve pipeline safety.  See 49 C.F.R. Part 192, Subpart P.  The 
DIMP regulations require pipeline operators to analyze their pipeline systems, 
circumstances, and programs to identify potential weaknesses that could result in high 
consequence accidents and to address those weaknesses before accidents occur.  Id.  
The DIMP regulations became effective February 2, 2010, and required gas companies 
to have a plan, i.e., a DIMP, implemented by August 2, 2011.  49 CFR § 192.1005(a).  
CNG’s completed its DIMP in May of 2011.  See 2013 CNG Rate Case Decision, p. 57.  
The Authority, through the Gas Pipeline Safety Unit (GPSU), has been involved with this 
rulemaking since its inception.  GPSU worked with the NGA and the Connecticut gas 
companies to ensure proper implementation of what is considered the largest set of new 
regulations affecting distribution companies since the Natural Gas Pipeline Safety Act of 
1968.  Id. 
The DIMP regulations promulgated by PHMSA are set as a baseline minimum 
safety level for the entire country.  See 49 C.F.R. Part 192, Subpart P.  Due to the 
significant variances between gas companies, their infrastructure, and their respective 
geographic regions, the DIMP regulations are mostly performance based in nature.  The 
DIMP regulations do not specifically state that the replacement of cast iron or bare steel 
pipe is required.  Id.  The regulations instead state that gas companies must: have 
knowledge of the systems; identify threats to the systems; evaluate and rank the risks; 
identify and implement measures to address the risks; measure performance; monitor 
and report results; evaluate effectiveness; and periodically evaluate and improve the 
program.  See 2013 CNG Rate Case Decision, pp. 57–58. 
One of the key elements of DIMP is the need to show improvement in the safety 
of the company’s system.  Decision, June 29, 2011, Docket No. 10-12-02, Application of 
Yankee Gas Services Company for Amended Rate Schedules (2010 YGS Rate Case 
Decision), p. 172.  Cast iron and bare steel piping are considered threats to safety 
because of leaks that are caused by several factors, including cracking of cast iron and 
corrosion of bare steel.  Id. 
According to the Company’s DIMP Plan, the highest ranked items in the 
Company’s overall threat ranking list all involve cast iron or bare steel piping.  Interrog. 
Resp. GPSU-023, Att. 1, App. C.  Based on these threats and the need to show 
improvement in reducing risk, the Company is requesting to fund its cast iron and bare 
steel pipe replacement program at a level to achieve completion of all work within the 
original 20-year replacement cycle.  Capital Investment Panel PFT, p. 33.  The 20-year

Conceptually, the DIMP program and associated DIMP rate mechanism have 
some similarities to the water companies’ Water Infrastructure and Conservation 
Adjustment (WICA) program.  Both programs address mains that require replacement by 
allowing for a rate mechanism that provides advance cost recovery outside of a rate case.  
However, in terms of cost recovery, the WICA program differs from the gas DIMP program 
in that the WICA program is statutorily authorized, and has cost recovery thresholds in

4. Earnings Sharing Mechanism 
An ESM is a ratemaking mechanism that shares a utility’s earnings in excess of its 
allowed ROE between the utility’s ratepayers and its shareholders.  The Authority 
established an ESM for CNG in the 2013 CNG Rate Case Decision.  2013 CNG Rate 
Case Decision, p. 111.  Under the Company’s approved ESM, the Company is required 
to split any earnings above its allowed ROE in any calendar year equally between the gas 
company’s ratepayers and shareholders, i.e., 50% to ratepayers and 50% to 
shareholders.  Id. 
The Company shall continue its ESM with a 50/50 split from the first dollar of over-
earnings above the allowed ROE.  Additionally, the Authority directs the Company to 
calculate the ROE using the lesser of the: (a) authorized debt and equity capitalization; 
or (b) the actual carried equity position, and to apply ESM carrying costs as of January 1 
of the subsequent year.  In addition, the Company is directed to separately identify and 
exclude all disallowed costs from its most recent rate case from ESM reporting on a going 
forward basis, and to provide an affirmation of the accuracy of its disallowed expenses.  
Going forward, the Authority will approve the Company’s annual ESM filings, subject to a 
full prudency review in the Company’s next rate case.  This guidance will allow for the 
Company to achieve its authorized ROE based on its authorized capital structure while 
ensuring that the Company shares excess earnings with ratepayers in accordance with 
the rate case decision.  This approach will also ensure that customers are not negatively 
impacted in situations where the Company incurs expenses related to projects, programs, 
or other items not approved in directives or orders outlined in this Decision. 
5. Hurdle Rate Calculation Methodology 
The Hurdle Rate Calculation Methodology is a financial model used by the LDCs 
to determine whether the expected revenue contribution from a new customer is sufficient 
to meet the minimum required LDC-specific rate of return on capital investments that is 
necessary to connect the customer to the system.  If the new customer’s contribution is 
less than the underlying connection costs, the customer must provide a contribution in 
aid of construction payment to recover the shortfall.  The length of the payback period in 
the Hurdle Rate Calculation Methodology determines whether the new customer or the 
LDC’s ratepayers pay more of the costs required to connect the new customer to the 
system.

6. Purchased Gas Adjustment Clause 
The Authority established the PGA clause “to allow [LDCs] to charge or to 
reimburse the consumer only for the changes in the cost of purchased gas which occur 
when the actual price of purchased gas differs from the price reflected in the base rates 
of the company.”  General Statutes, § 16-19b(b); see also Decision, June 30, 1977, 
Docket No. 76-03-07, Decision on Purchased Gas Adjustment Clause.  The Authority 
monitors and oversees the application of the PGA clause “to determine whether charges 
or credits made under such clauses reflect the actual prices paid for purchased gas or 
energy and the actual transmission costs and are computed in accordance with the 
applicable clause.”  General Statutes § 16-19b(h). 
Purchased gas costs are offset by NFM revenue, as well as other recoveries.  NFM 
revenue is earned by LDCs through short-term off-system sales and capacity release 
transactions, and on-system interruptible sales and transportation activity.  Interrog. Resp. 
PURA-46, p. 1.  Since 2014, and until December 31, 2023, which is the date on which 
the SEP ended, LDCs have used the proceeds from the sales, i.e., NFM, to reduce the 
costs of gas through the PGA and to support the SEP.  See General Statutes § 16-
19ww(d)(4); see also Decision, Jan. 14, 2015, Docket No. 13-06-02RE01, PURA

The Company did not propose a usage cap for LIDR.  Rate Design and Cost of 
Service Panel PFT, p. 25.  According to the Company, it considered implementing a

process and might confuse customers.  Id.  However, the Company can create systems 
to implement multiple monthly usage caps to accommodate seasonal variation.  Interrog. 
Resp. EOE-370.  Introducing a monthly cap on discounted usage could raise 
implementation costs by about $40,000, provided the hardship qualification criteria 
remain unchanged and no additional customer communication is needed.  Id., p. 2.

and the seasonal nature of gas usage can be mitigated or eliminated.  EOE Brief, p. 47.

EOE argues that the Company’s concerns about customer confusion are overstated, as 
customers can understand that discounts apply to a limited amount of usage, encouraging 
energy efficiency to reduce overall gas charges.  Id.  Therefore, effective communication, 
as approved for the EDC LIDR, can address this issue.  Id. 
EOE also suggests that the complexity and seasonality concerns can be mitigated 
by establishing seasonal usage caps within the system to reflect typical gas usage 
patterns.  Id.  As such, EOE recommends that the Authority require the Company to 
implement seasonal usage caps of 100 ccf for November through April and 30 ccf for May 
through October.  EOE Brief, p. 47.  EOE asserts that evidence supports the inclusion of 
usage caps, as shown by data indicating that some hardship customers use more than 
double the average amount.  Id.; see Late Filed Ex. 152, Att. 1.  There is no justification

conservation goals, making it unreasonable for other ratepayers to subsidize such usage.

OCC supports reasonable cost control measures, including usage caps, but notes 
concern regarding fairness and price signals.  OCC Brief, p. 172.  Specifically, some 
customers may not control their usage or have access to energy efficiency measures.  Id.  
Therefore, OCC does not propose a usage cap for the Rate Year but recommends that 
the Authority consider usage caps in future evaluations of gas discount rates.  Id.  To 
support this evaluation, OCC recommends that the Company tracks the usage of LIDR-
enrolled customers and compare it to past usage to assess whether the LIDR incentivizes 
increased usage.  OCC Brief, p. 173. 
The Authority concurs with OCC's recommendation that more data is needed to 
ensure a fair and reasonable usage cap for qualifying customers.  Therefore, once the 
Company implements LIDR, tracking the usage of LIDR-enrolled customers will be crucial 
in developing an appropriate usage cap.  The Authority also acknowledges that some 
LIDR-enrolled customers, particularly renters, may not have control over their energy 
usage or access to energy efficiency measures.  Nonetheless, cost control is essential to 
ensure fairness for all customers, including those not enrolled in LIDR.  As such, the 
Authority may address the development of a usage cap in a future proceeding. 
Accordingly, the Authority directs the Company to track the monthly usage of LIDR-
enrolled customers and compare it to the usage of non-LIDR-enrolled customers.

suggestions to mitigate increased usage among LIDR-enrolled customers, in each annual
