Offerings.

Company incurs a $1.00 fee per check, totaling $595 in 2022.  Id.  For electronic 
automated clearing house (ACH) payment returns, the fee ranges from $0.050 to $5.00 
depending on the reason, with a total expense of $4,673 in 2022.  Id.  Overall, the total 
expense for returned checks and ACH payments in 2022 was $5,268.  Id.  The Company 
reported $214,000 in return check fee revenue for the Test Year and proposed $198,000

returned payments and that customers whose payments are declined should bear those 
costs.  OCC Brief, p. 178.  However, OCC opposes adding extra disincentives to deter 
bad checks, as current collection policies already encourage customers to pay their gas 
bills.  Id.  The Company should not charge more than their operating costs, in line with 
General Statutes § 16-19e(a)(4).  Id.  Given the varying fees for processing bad checks, 
OCC recommends capping the fee charged to customers at the Company's maximum 
per-transaction cost of $5.00 for administrative efficiency and clarity.  Id. 
The Authority acknowledges that the Company is not proposing to increase the 
current returned check fee and that the proposed revenue for the Rate Year is lower than 
the Test Year.  See Late Filed Ex. 1 Att. 2, Sch. C-3.01b WP.  Nonetheless, the Authority 
agrees with OCC that the Company should not charge more than its operating costs.  
Therefore, any future request to increase the returned check fee must be structured in 
such a way that the Company receives no more than the Company’s operating costs 
relating to such fees.  See General Statutes § 16-19e(a)(4).

EOE-44; Interrog. Resp. EOE-46; Interrog. Resp. EOE-47; Interrog. Resp. EOE-313; 
Interrog. Resp. EOE-314; Interrog. Resp. EOE-315; Interrog. Resp. EOE-316; Interrog. 
Resp. EOE-407; Interrog. Resp. EOE-472.  One major issue is that the Company fails to 
consistently ask customers the financial hardship pre-qualification questions, despite four 
years of guidelines, scripts, and penalties from the Authority.  EOE Brief, p. 26.  In 5% of 
the reviewed calls, the Company missed the opportunity to prequalify customers for 
financial hardship, delaying the assistance these customers needed.  Id.  Additionally, 
when pre-qualification did occur, the Company sometimes failed to inform customers that 
they could submit income information if they do not receive government benefits or lack 
documentation of their government benefits.  Id.  This omission could result in customers 
not receiving the correct benefits due to an incomplete or inaccurate understanding of the 
requirements.  Id. 
EOE notes that a recurring issue among Avangrid companies is their tendency to 
prioritize medical protection questions over financial hardship designations.  EOE Brief, 
p. 27; see also Interrog. Resp. EOE-44; Interrog. Resp. EOE-316.  EOE explained that 
financial hardship status is crucial as it offers special payment arrangements and federal 
assistance, benefiting both the customer and ratepayers.  EOE Brief, p. 27.  As such, 
relying solely on medical protection, which can allow service continuation without 
payment, can be outdated given the many available assistance options.  Id. 
The Company struggled to explain the relationship between hardship, energy 
assistance (CEAP), and payment arrangements correctly.  EOE Brief, p. 27.  For instance, 
it incorrectly stated that receiving CEAP was a prerequisite for a hardship designation.  
Id.; see also Interrog. Resp. EOE-43; Interrog. Resp. EOE-44.  The Company also 
misunderstood the interaction between financial hardship and the matching payment plan 
(MPP) and failed to recognize that CEAP-eligible customers at a previous address would 
likely qualify for financial hardship status at a new address.  EOE Brief, p. 27.  Additionally, 
the Company inaccurately explained the hardship process and paperwork, told at least 
one customer that hardship designations were unavailable at certain times of the year, 
and mishandled hardship documentation and account coding.  Id. 
Regarding payment arrangements, the Company made several errors.  It 
incorrectly informed a customer that paying extra would break their payment arrangement 
and gave another customer the wrong payment amount and due date.  EOE Brief, p. 27; 
see also Interrog. Resp. EOE-476.  Additionally, the Company failed to adequately explain 
payment arrangements, did not clarify reasons for failed arrangements, and misinformed 
customers about MPP eligibility.  EOE Brief, p. 27.  In one instance, the Company 
attempted to place a customer on the wrong payment arrangement, claiming they were 
ineligible for MPP and trying to switch them to a flexible payment arrangement.  Id.

a. Credit and Collection Calls to Alorica 
The Company proposed insourcing 35% of its credit and collection customer call 
activity to mirror the insourcing directive for UI in the 2023 Rate Case Decision.  Customer 
Service Panel PFT, pp. 53–54.  The Company’s projected incremental cost increase of 
$1.61 million is based on historical call volume trends and expected costs to outsource 
other call types.  Id., p. 56.  However, on March 13, 2024, the Company informed the 
Authority that it was transitioning all credit and collection calls away from iQor and to 
Alorica.  Customer Service Panel Supp. Rebuttal, pp. 2, 4, 6. 
EOE contends that the Company’s various adjustments to its revenue 
requirements makes the actual costs unclear.  EOE Brief, p. 43.  Additionally, EOE 
highlights discrepancies in the Company's CSR headcount and associated costs, pointing 
out that the Company used varying cost estimates, which complicates the evaluation of 
true savings.  Id.  EOE argues that despite concerns about the Alorica contract mirroring 
iQor's negative aspects, transitioning all calls to Alorica for a one-year rate case could 
determine if vendor issues are the main reason for the Company’s customer service 
problems.  Id.  As this proceeding involves a one-year rate case, EOE believes the best 
financial option is to transition all credit and collection calls to Alorica to determine if 
vendor issues are the root of customer service problems.  Id., pp. 43–44.  This approach 
allows for a quick pivot, if necessary, whereas insourcing might not resolve issues if the 
Company itself is the problem.  EOE Brief, pp. 43–44. 
As of May 23, 2024, the Company testified that “as of today, 100 percent of the 
credit and collections calls are outsourced.  Those calls are currently handled by [iQor] 
and are due to be transitioned over to Alorica.  We're in the process of transferring 100 
percent of those calls . . . from [iQor] to Alorica.”  CNG Hr’g Tr., May 23, 2024, 2065:2–8.  
Alorica will be assigned 100% of credit and collections calls by the end of September 
2024.  Tr., 2096:8–25.

2. Customer Experience Activities 
Since the Company’s last rate case, several enhancements have been made to 
improve the performance and features of the Company’s digital platforms to enhance the 
overall customer experience.  Customer Service Panel PFT, p. 28.  The Company’s 
website migrated to a new cloud-based platform, providing a more stable and robust 
experience that scales based on customer traffic, especially during high-demand periods 
like storms.  Id.  This scalability supports the growing preference for self-service among 
digital customers.  Id., p. 29. 
In 2019, the Company launched a mobile app, allowing customers to manage their 
accounts easily and on their own.  Id.  The app features bill viewing and downloading, 
payments, transaction history, FAQs, and support.  Id.  The app also offers options like 
eBill enrollment, AutoPay, and Budget Billing.  Id.  By the end of 2022, the app had a 31% 
download rate for CNG customers.  Id.  As of August 2023, the CNG app had a 4.6 star 
rating with 889 ratings.  Id. 
CNG customers receiving electronic bills have a 27-point higher satisfaction score 
than those receiving mailed statements.  Customer Service Panel PFT, p. 29.  The 
Company asserts that utilizing eBill also encourages the use of other self-service tools 
available through online accounts.  Id. 
In 2023, the Company implemented the Net Promoter Score (NPS) metric to gauge 
customer experience in real-time across their digital platforms and phone interactions.  
Customer Service Panel PFT, p. 30.  After a transaction is completed, customers have 
the opportunity to provide detailed feedback in response to the standard NPS question, 
"[h]ow likely are you to recommend [Company] to a friend?"  Id.  This assists the Company 
in identifying areas for improvement and provides the opportunity to monitor Company 
performance.  Id. 
The Company plans to use NPS as one of several metrics to assess an agent's 
overall performance.  Interrog. Resp. CAE-42.  By incorporating NPS, the Company can 
track a quantitative trend at the agent level based on customer feedback.  Id.  The 
Company can review the related calls and provide additional training or take other 
necessary actions.  Id.  After the call, customers are routed to a survey where they answer 
the standard NPS question and five other questions.  Interrog. Resp. CAE-41.  The survey 
collects customer ratings, a customer identifier, transaction date, and the assisting agent.  
Id.  This data is stored in a dataset and used to develop a dashboard displaying all NPS 
data.  Id.  This dashboard helps operational managers, quality assurance managers, 
product developers, and customer experience analysts analyze performance and identify 
improvement opportunities.  Id.  If customers provide detailed comments with their NPS
